messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had been working the late shift at a shopping center in Auckland when the accident happened. She was sixty-one, single, and proud of the way she had always been able to keep order as a security guard, moving quietly through car parks and entrances while the mall emptied for the night. On that evening, a delivery driver had argued with a store employee near a loading bay, and in the confusion Marisol had stepped in, trying to separate them and call for backup. What she intended as a firm hold turned suddenly into a stumble; the man fell hard against the concrete edge of a curb, and when Marisol saw his head strike, the scene broke open in an instant. He ended up with a serious injury, and Marisol was left staring at the blood and the stunned faces around her, unable to understand how a routine shift had become something irreversible.

In the weeks that followed, what troubled her most was how little of it she could properly hold onto. There were parts of the event that she simply could not remember no matter how hard she tried, and the missing sections frightened her because she felt they should explain what had gone wrong. Other moments came back in fragments—his body slipping, the sound of someone shouting, the look on a supervisor’s face—but even when she could recall what happened, it often felt as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. At times she would picture the scene and feel completely numb, as if she were describing an incident that had happened to a stranger. Because the memory felt broken and unreal, Marisol found herself returning to it again and again, thinking about why the event had happened to her and dwelling on what she had done wrong. She overanalysed every detail, from where she had placed her hands to whether she had moved too quickly, hoping that if she could reconstruct the missing pieces she would finally understand how she had caused such harm.

That searching only made the memory more troublesome. The more Marisol tried to make sense of it, the more she noticed the blank spaces, and those gaps seemed to sharpen her sense that there must have been a fatal mistake hidden inside them. She would go over the scene late at night, replaying each second and then stopping at the same empty places, unable to retrieve what her mind refused to give back. The loss of certainty pushed her further into self-blame rumination: if she could not remember everything, she assumed she must have missed something important, and if she had missed something important, then she must be responsible. Even the parts she could recall grew more alien under that pressure, as though the event were separating from her own life and becoming a case she could never solve. That made her think harder still, and the harder she thought, the less settled the memory felt.

At work, the consequences began to spill outward. Marisol stayed on edge during shifts at the shopping center, especially near the loading bays and entrances where arguments or sudden movement could happen. She became preoccupied with reviewing her actions, replaying decisions while she patrolled, and that constant mental replay left her exhausted and distracted. She started avoiding situations that reminded her of the incident, stepping back from conflict whenever she could and shrinking her role into tasks that felt safer. Over time she found herself less willing to take on busy areas of the mall, and the confidence she had once brought to the job gave way to hesitation. She would still walk the corridors in uniform, but inside she was often back at the curb, turning the same questions over and over: what had she done wrong, what had she failed to see, why had that moment been hers.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was barely sleeping and was worn down by the strain of carrying both the missing pieces and the explanations she kept forcing into them. She said she came because she could not stop thinking about the injury she had caused, and because each attempt to understand it only seemed to pull her deeper into the same loop. What she feared most was that the broken memory meant there was something unforgivable she would never recover, and what she hoped for, though she was almost embarrassed to say it, was some way to hold the event without feeling as if she were forever watching a stranger ruin her life.
